Room 401, presentation day. The projector fan whirs. Some students are here to watch the presentation but most are falling asleep.
Balcony of Building A, night. Campus lights glow in the distance. Jessa leans on the rail with her sleeves over her hands.

Room 401, a week later. Rain on the window.
Balcony of Building A, night. A respectful distance between you.

Room 401, afternoon. Jessa is waving a cup of milk tea around while telling a story. The cup tips. It heads straight for Inna's planner.
Library, late afternoon. A free hour, a window seat, and a quiet reading room.
Library, evening. The reading room is almost empty. Inna is tallying the club's funds on the back of a flyer, lips moving.
Room 401, after rehearsal. You ask Inna to explain a slide a second time.

Room 401, afternoon. Inna has made a spreadsheet and a backup spreadsheet. Nikka is auditing both. Jessa is eating chips.
A narrow street in Vigan, morning. The family stall is half open; frying oil and calamansi in the air. Apong Pasing sits on a stool; Migo, Inna's younger brother, reads a comic on an upturned crate.
Inna's family house. A small back room with boxes and a table half-covered in notes. Inna folds the same cardboard box three times.
Inna's family house, late afternoon, after the interview. Inna slips between languages as she goes: Ilokano with Migo, Taglish with you, careful English for her planner.

Room 401, a few days later. Students drift in for the next meeting.

Room 401, after rehearsal. You ask Nikka a string of simple questions about the schedule. She decides to answer in the shortest possible way.

A riverside market in Naga, morning. Stalls under blue tarps, wet cobbles, a shouting jeepney. Nikka carries a notebook; you carry the recorder.

Nikka's family house, early evening. A small table by a window that looks onto the river. Field notes are spread across it. Nikka's mother passes through with a tray and a look that says "eat something."

Room 401, presentation morning. Nikka has laid out her cue cards in an exact semicircle. Jessa is trying to rearrange them.

Admissions office, morning. A ceiling fan ticks. An application form waits on the counter.
Next student please! Here’s your acknowledgement receipt and… Oh? You’re that one student transferee from the CICS department, aren’t you?
Thank you po… Oh uhm yeah, that’s me. Am I… that known already?

Oh, don’t worry ‘nak. I just remember you distinctly since I never thought somebody would choose “The Filipino Language and its Dialects” for their club. Usually, kids like you opt for the more gizmo-whiz-something stuff!
Ah, that’s why… I have always wanted to know more about our different languages and—
Well anyways! Enough about that. Just sign your name in the sheet and you’ll officially be part of the club!
What is your first name?
What is your last name?
What nickname would you like to use?
Mx. [LAST NAME], you have a nice name! Well then, the club room is in Building A - Room 401. Enjoy the rest of the semester, especially considering the girls are a rambunctious bunch.
R-rambunctious?
Oh you’ll see dear!
As you walk through the unfamiliar buildings of this familiar campus, you wonder how this fall semester of second year will change the wind of the following months.
Building A, Room 401, but soon will be known as home. A flight of stairs, then a door already open. Three overlapping voices leak into the hallway.
Don’t call me a thief! It’s just chairs, if I was feeling a bit more devious, I would’ve stolen their IDs!
It was daylight robbery, Jessa. You didn’t even ask the prof to borrow some— you blatantly stole two chairs under his nose.
Correction: Three. Can’t you count? I do believe it's more concerning how she managed to carry all that despite being 148—
HEY! That’s irrelevant—
The rambunctious voices came to a halt when somebody— you— opened the door.
Uh. Hello po? Is this the language club?
Woah woah woah! A new member? I could’ve sworn my seniors told me that this club was not a hot spot for students but suddenly we’re four?!?!?!?
Jessa, tone it down. You’re scaring the newcomer.
Nikka, I fear it's too late. Can’t you see them backing out of the room?
Once again, the room stilled into silence. You awkwardly decide to hand them the receipt the staff gave you earlier to confirm that you are a member of the club as well.
Mx. [LAST NAME]? Grabe, ang pormal! I can’t believe somebody new decided to join this club of ours! Vice prezi, this calls for a celebration!!!!!
We don’t even have the funds to……… (sigh) I suppose a welcome is in order, [FIRST NAME].
Okay but before everything else, how do you want us to call you?
What do you want to be called?

column3: Just my first name. We're all clubmates naman.

column6: Hm. I suppose that’s fine.
Hala, so formal! “Boss” na lang tawag ko sa’yo. No buts!
[FIRST NAME] [FIRST NAME] [FIRST NAME]... I’ll remember your name from now on!
Easiest to remember considering it's the name we’ll first see.
Yay! We’ll be besties from now on, [NICKNAME]!!”
Okay, our introductions next! I'm Jessa, Jessa Villarin. I’m the club president and the very best around. ✌🏼
I’m Inna Agcaoili, the vice president. Here’s to a joyous semester together.
Nikka Roco, but you can just call me Nikka. I’m the club treasurer— oh! That would make you the secretary then.
Welcome to the club!
Room 401, after the orientation and casual discussions. The chairs in the classroom are formed in a circle, although four are only used. A whiteboard is set in the middle of the group.
We’re not a language club without the language, so for today’s task, let’s give our new addition a word!
… Did I do something wrong?
She didn’t mean it like that. Every week, we circle around and say a word in our own dialect.
I don’t think you’ve realized it yet but we’re from different areas in the Philippines. I personally am from Ilokos, Nikka is from Bikol, and Jessa is from Cebu.
Isn’t it amazing!? We’re all from different regions in the Philippines yet we still managed to wander up here! Oh, how about you boss? Where did you come from?
Where did you come from?
[ADDRESS] you say? It’s unbelievable to think about how we all managed to meet here now despite our distance.
It’s kinda like fate !! / It’s kind of like fate?
?!??!?! Nikka hey !!!
Predictable as ever.
The two girls began chasing around each other in the room while Inna stood there deadpanned. This seems to be a common experience in the club.
Room 401, Jessa sits in front of you while the other two discuss amongst themselves in the corner.
I’m so sorry about the fuss! Nikka really knows how to get me going I swear!!
It’s alright, I don’t really mind.
Aww thank y—
Suddenly, Jessa sat up straight and looked at you expectantly.
Salamat kaayo.
What??
Hehe… It’s kind of like thank you but given with more gratitude. You already know Salamat since it's the same in Tagalog though.
Then kaayo would mean…?
It would mean “... very, very much.” See the emphasis now?
What does "Salamat kaayo" mean?
Awh! You’re very very veryyyy much welcome too, bossing!
Almost!!! You missed the “kaayo” [NICKNAME]!!
Hey now you’re being a little too advanced than who you’re talking with !!
Room 401. Inna sits a little apart, notebook squared to the desk edge.
A word with no context is just a sound, so here's a word for you. Agyamanak. It means "thank you," or more exactly "I thank you."
Is it casual?
No no… It's more polite and sincere. With family, you say it quicker while with someone you respect, say it fully and clearly. (a beat) See how context affects a word?
I see... Agyamanak.
Say it slower. Again.
In addition, you can add apo to show respect. For example: Agyamanak, apo.
What does "Agyamanak" mean?
Correct, I’m glad you’re a rather quick learner… Not that it would be bad if you made a mistake though… Ahem. Anyways, you’re welcome.
That’s incorrect, even though it’s close. Agyamanak is more polite, so Thank you is the better term.
Ah. Don’t apologize, it’s alright to not immediately get the term correct… Oh that was your guess? (a beat) I’m… sorry.
Room 401. Nikka sits across from you, one foot on a chair.
Most people would learn a phrase and assume they know the whole story from just that.
There’s usually a context to better understand the situation no?
Bingo. Look at this: Marhay na aga or to you, it’s "Good morning" or Magandang araw. But in a market, it could also mean: I see you, the day has started, we're both here.
From a two word translation to a full sentence…
See how context matters before the word settles? That’s what I like about language— how it changes into something you need at the moment.
Marhay na aga.
Hah! (small smile) Dai man maraot. Not bad. Unfortunately, it’s already noon.
When would you say "Marhay na aga"?

column3: To greet someone in the morning.

column6: Yes but remember who says it first. People can tell you a lot with the right timing.
You should always greet somebody first before immediately asking questions, you know?
It could work if you’re being sarcastic, otherwise, incorrect.
Library. Late afternoon. A quiet corner with a single carrel and a green-shaded lamp. A small sign: STUDY BREAK AVAILABLE.
Three new words in your notebook. Three people whose voices you can already hear when you read them back.
Welcome to the Library Hub. Study Breaks are solo scripted quizzes for downtime. Progress through the story to receive more study strategies.
STUDY BREAK (tutorial). Review: Salamat kaayo, Agyamanak, Marhay na aga.
Match "Agyamanak" to its meaning.
Which word means "good morning" in Central Bikol?
Write the Cebuano phrase for "thank you very much."
column10: it starts with the word you share with Tagalog.

column6: Your notebook feels different now. Heavier. In a good way.
You can review these words or repeat this study break.
Before you leave
Room 401, a week later. A projector hums to life as the club advisor presents a powerpoint to the screen with the words “Language in Everyday Life.”
Okay, club, quiet muna. I know how fun it’s been to just mingle around with each other during the beginning week but it’s now time to officially start the club activities.

You guys will be doing a project named: Language in Everyday Life. You will be paired into two members and you are tasked to experience your chosen language in its everyday occurrence. You will need to include a small vocab set and examples of the language in context. After that, you’ll write a reflection on what you learned throughout the project.

Optionally, you can visit yourself the areas where your chosen dialect is more common in usage. It would just be paid by your own pocket though, but I’ll give extra credit to those who do in-person research. Do you understand the task everyone?
Yes, Ma'am!!
(whispering) Hey hey! Let’s partner up, it’ll be fun trust me! I know a lot of people who can help us ace this!!
(whispering) If you want to partner with me then just say so, I promise to present something amazing.
(whispering) Oh? Choose me as your partner if you want but I don’t like partners who are pabigat, alright?
(thinking) Hm… I should choose somebody that I feel like I’ll really get along with.
Choose your project partner
Wait, really? You chose me? Okay okay okay. (to the other two) Sorry!!Yyou can't have the club's newest member. Ma’am, do we get additional points for being the first group to form!?
No.
Thanks for choosing me [NICKNAME]. I’ll try my best to send the task assignment later once I get home. I hope you don’t mind?
I won’t, don’t worry.
(A small smile) Agyamanak, [FIRST NAME].
Oh wow. Okay. (blinks, then half a smile) You better pull your weight alright, I’m not one to take excuses.
I figured.
You learn quickly, Mx. [LAST NAME].
Jessa fills every silence before it can land. The MC learns when to laugh with her, when to ask what she means, and when to leave the gap open.
Settings: Library, Classroom, Street/Stalls (Cebu), Home (Cebu), Balcony.
A corner table by the window with sticky notes everywhere. A sign says QUIET PLEASE, which Jessa has ignored twice already.
Okay, team meeting— although we’re only two members. Anyways, let’s discuss the distribution for tasks. I’ll be in charge of the food and you’ll be the team leader!
Why is the new guy the team leader…? Not to mention you forgot to distribute the tasks for the project?
Ah- Right, the project. Sorry, I haven’t eaten breakfast yet...
OH! Since it’s lunch time soon, I have an idea!
First assignment for the project muna kasi I'm a responsible researcher now. DYK, in Cebuano we have two kinds of "we." 🤓☝️

Kita means we and that means you're included. Kami means we but it doesn’t count you.. So Kaon ta! is "let's eat," meaning you're invited. While Mokaon mi is "we're eating," and you're just third wheeling our group!
So one little word decides if included or not?
I know right? One wrong word immediately ditches you like that! Petty sobrang petty!
Invite Jessa to lunch, including her. Type the Cebuano.
Nice you included yourself! Finally lunch— or well, brunch since I haven’t eaten yet? It’s my treat for answering so well!
Awh man, you got it wrong. It’s “Kaon ta!” … Don’t worry, let’s go get lunch either way. You’re treating me though!
Room 401. The club PC freezes on Jessa's title slide.
No, no, no, no... come on, just load please— you were working five minutes ago—
(The progress bar stops. She jabs the keyboard.)
Unsa man diay ni?! Ayaw, ayaw, ayaw!
(She slaps the desk. The room freezes. A chair squeaks.)
O-oh, I didn’t realize you’re here… I’m sorry. That was loud.
Was that... Cebuano?
She said "what even is this." (a beat) The rest was prayer.
It was NOT prayer. It was… more of a persuasion tactic.
More like begging.
HEY!!!
Unsa man diay ni? Does that mean “What even is this?”
(blinks, then slowly grins) You understood that? Okay. That's embarrassing. And also kinda sweet. I can’t believe my student is learning!
How do you answer?

column3: Calm down. It's just a slide.

column6: You will? Awwww thank you so much! My life saver ever!!
Hey! That’s not a way to treat your senior!! (she's laughing too)
Ah. (a short breath) You’re right… It’s just a slide.
Late afternoon. You have a free hour and a quiet carrel with a green lamp.
STUDY BREAK — Cebuano: Interjections and Particles. Five items from the dictionary database.
Hala! is used when someone is...
Which word means "I don't know"?
Write "What?" in Cebuano.
Arrange the cards to mean "What am I going to do about this?" Cards: ko / Unsaon / ni.
Lagot ka! most closely means...
Study Break complete. New: Ambot, Unsa, Unsaon ko ni, Lagot ka.
You close the lamp. Somewhere across campus, a projector sighs in Cebuano.
Library, evening. The reading room is almost empty except for Jessa is rearranging sticky notes into a calendar on the table.
(She mutters, not noticing that you have sat down nearby.)
Asa na man to... asa na man to... Unsaon ko ni? (she moves one note, then another, then covers her face) ...Hayst.
Gimingaw ko kang Lola.
(She goes still. Then straightens as if the sentence never happened.)
Oh! Hi! Didn't see you. How long have you been there?
Unsaon ko ni. What do I do with this? (gently) It seems like the problem doesn’t seem to be just the sticky notes…
(a long pause) ...Maybe, it’s just that... Yeah sorry.
Not long. You were talking to the notes.
They listen better than most people. They’re like mini journals of my thoughts. Hmm… On that note.
(She pretends to scribble something but her eyes aren't on them.)
Room 401, after a project meeting. You lean on Jessa's laptop and accidentally close it.
Ay. Ay! Lagot ka, lagot ka, lagot ka kay Lola! (sing-song, dancing around you) I'm telling her!
What does that even mean?
It means I have power over you. (grinning) And that you owe me a snack.
Lagot ka? I know that one. (smirking) Lagot ka rin, Jessa. You left your charger in the library still plugged!
(a gasp) Ah damn it! My secret has been exposed! Tell the librarian I didn’t mean it pleaseee… (laughing) I’m so proud of you though, doing research behind my back!
(a pause) Don’t worry, I wasn't mad about the slide.
I know.
You know me so well.
Library, evening. Inna's usual table is buried in club papers. The librarian's desk has a laminated sign: SILENCE IS GOLDEN. Jessa has been reading it out loud for a full minute.
Silence is golden. (whispering, very loudly) Gold is expensive though. Nikka, how much does our silence cost?
(without looking up from her ledger) Fifty pesos per sentence, amount payable to the club treasurer.
Please don't encourage her.
Okay okay okay, I'll whisper. Watch. (whispering) Boss, are you ready for the next vocab list?
(Her whisper carries across the whole reading room. The librarian looks up. All four of you freeze.)
Shh.
(tiny) Sorry po. Hinay-hinay na ko.
Hinay-hinay?
It means like… "slowly" or "gently." Like when Lola tells you to put the plate down softly. Or not to run on the wet floor. Or to calm down. Hinay-hinay lang,.
So it's not "shut up."
NEVER. It's basically "easy lang." The softer way.
She learned it by being told it a lot.
Wow. The treasurer is bullying me again.
It’s an observation more than anything.
Tell Jessa to take it slowly.
column10: say it twice, like a heartbeat.

column6: (placing a hand over her heart) Hinay-hinay lang. Woah, that sounded so gentle. Say it again when I panic, please. Very ASMR.
Almost! It's the same word twice. Hinay. Hinay. (she bobs her head) Like a slow waltz.
Would you like a tutor session with Jessa?
In the library at the corner table. Jessa has brought a paper bag and is hiding something behind it.

Tutor time! Let’s set some rules, rule one: No english for you. You can’t learn if you rely too much on familiar language. Rule two: Each wrong answer means you need to treat me to food for a day in the canteen!
Hey that’s—
Rule one! Unless you wanna treat me so badly.
Okay let’s begin; the words I chose are very relevant too! Gutom is hungry. Busog is full. Lami is delicious.
And kapoy is Tired. You probably know those english words already though.
Gutom, busog, lami, kapoy.
Well, now I really want you to get it wrong. This is aking me hungry!
Tell Jessa you're hungry.
Gigutom ko too! Let’s go get some food in our system then!
Close! Try "ko" after the hungry word. "Ko" is "I." Meaning I’m hungry!
Tell Jessa the snack is very delicious.
Kapoy na pud ko...
(She looks up quickly.)
Don't translate that. It's a secret. (grinning) Nah, kidding aside, it just means "I'm tired again."
I’m glad you’re learning so well. Next week will be our in-person research too so the fact you’ve gotten the hang of it is… Nice.
How do you answer?
Woah! You’ve been doing your research huh? (An awkward laugh) Nimo is for saying things to a single person while sa tanan is for everything.
You’re basically telling me—
Thank you so much for everything.
You make it sound like I did something crazy… (Looks away) Way sapayan. You’re welcome.
I’m glad my student finally knows respect!
Don’t tell me you’re only learning for the project!?
Room 401, afternoon. Nikka has a ledger and a calculator she doesn't need. Jessa is sitting on a desk, which is not a chair. Inna is making a color-coded list on the whiteboard.
Okay, I believe its time for the club budget meeting. Ma’am said the in-person trips are paid out of our own pockets, so I did the math.
AGH! Math, and so early in the day!? My poor ears !!!
We would need money for transportation, food, and Jessa’ impulsive shopping sprees.
Hey don’t put a tax on my motivation!
Motivation is questionable if it’s a 300 lost on the first day.

(ignores) It would be a total of around three thousand five hundred for the total expenses. It’s best to make your money’s worth by actually doing the project and wasting time treating this as a vacation. Got it, children?
(They all look at you. You weren't expecting to be the one deciding.)
Hey boss, don't stress about it! You don't have to say yes right now. Lola will cook, and my tita's cousin has extra mats, so no hotel! You just bring yourself and transportation money!
How do you answer?

column3: I'll go. I want to hear the language where it lives.

column6: YAY! (then, quieter) Thank you. Really. It means a lot that you'd go all that way for this.
Pay your share by Friday, Mx. [LAST NAME].
(dry) You’re too obsessed with money, Nikka.
I said that because I'm the treasurer. Nothing more, or less.
Oh, it’s alright, trust me (she hops off the desk) I’m the club president so I’m in charge with making sure my clubmates are all accounted for. With that, I’m using the class funds to treat you!
She didn’t even do that when I needed money. (flatly) I'll log it as a "donation." Sliding scale.
That's… actually very kind of you, Jessa.
Why would I give you money if I don’t know where you’re using it!
Don’t make it sound weird.
Of course! Sleep on it, boss. Lola isn't going anywhere. She's been there for forty years.
(Nikka writes your name in pencil. Not pen. You notice.)
Cebuano streets. A busy roadside in Cebu at noon. Lola Ising sits behind a food stall under a blue tarp as cousin Yani wipes the counter.
La! This is [PLAYER NAME], my project partner! They’re the new club member and my favorite student.
Aaah. Iha, don’t treat your friends like they’re your students. [PLAYER NAME], sit. Kaon.
(She puts a plate in front of you.)
(whispering) She already decided she likes you. Don't ruin it.
Lami?
Lami kaayo, La.

Good. (turning the planner toward you) Write something in the margin. Anything. To remember this day.
(You write: "Thursday afternoon. Step. Intayon.")
Weeks later. Her planner has a blank square every week. The squares aren't empty. They just aren't assigned.
THE THINGS WE CHOOSE (ROMANTIC)
Room 401, a few days later. Students drift in for the next meeting.
I thought about what you said. I appreciate that you didn't need an answer.
I mean it. I'm just glad to know you, from a clubmate to now a friend. This is the best choice.
You’ll see your name in my planner often. The project may have ended but you’re still my friend, we should plan the next hangout.
A last word

column3: Save me a seat in the library then.

column6: Thursday afternoon is open, if you want it.
Section C, third table. It's already reserve.
A PLACE BESIDE ME (CLASSMATES ONLY)
Library, closing time. The two of you stand a polite distance apart.
(very gently) I need to be honest. I don't feel the same way, and I don't want to answer out of obligation.
Thank you for telling me honestly.
I'm learning that a clear no is kinder than a polite maybe. I don’t want to lead you on, I’m sorry.
A last word

column3: It's okay. Thank you for choosing your own answer.
I'd still like to be your clubmate.

column6: (soft) That's the nicest thing anyone's said to me this month.
I'd like that too. I'll save you the third table.
MY OWN ANSWER (REJECTION)
Library, afternoon. A back table by the bookshelf. Nikka has a field notebook open and a sketch of the campus with three question marks drawn on it.
Okay, Mx. [LAST NAME]. Let’s start with five questions. One: what do you want this project to be about?
Everyday talk, maybe? How do people use a language without thinking about it in their daily life?
Two: who gets to decide what's "everyday"?
...Hold on. That’s a hypothetical—
Three: whose everyday? Four: how do we know we're not just hearing what they expect us to need? Five: are your legs not tired? Sit down. We’ll be here for a while.
You ask WAY too many questions.
Don’t we need a solid foundation before starting with the project? It helps us track down our work timeline without confusing ourselves about the delegated tasks. Clever, isn’t it?
Uh-huh…
Okay, you are NOT catching my drift. Alright then, let’s just start with something simple: Questions.
We have the 5 W’s and H questions in English and Tagalog. We also obviously have these in Bicolano too, the common ones are: Ano? is "what." Siisay? is "who." Sain? is "where." Taano? is "why."
Taano is the best one for me though, as it questions everything, even a bad idea.
Taano?
(a flicker of pleasure) Why? Well why not? Nothing’s wrong with questioning more about the world.
Ask "Why?" in Bikol.
column10: it starts with the same sound as "tanong."

column6: Yes. Use it sparingly though. People get nervous if you keep pushing them like that.
Why did you get it wrong?
Room 401, afternoon. Nikka has drawn a map of the building on the whiteboard in careful, colored marker. A classmate leans on the board while talking and smears half of it.
(Nikka stares at the smear. A beat. Then:)
Ay, taano man?! Dai! Dai! (she grabs the eraser from his hand) Likot mo naman!
(The classmate retreats, hands up. Nikka exhales through her nose.)
(whispering to you) Don't worry about her. She’s not really angry, but also is? She’s very particular I suppose.
...Sorry. That was a lot.
What did you say?
She said "why" and "no," and that was the polite version.
A rather sparingly polite version if anything.
Taano man. Why, though? (gently) Don’t accidentally throw the eraser, Nikka. The poor guy retreated already.
(a short pause, then a quick, surprised laugh) Hah! Flaunting your knowledge with only a couple of words known? I see what you’re doing.
What do you do?

column3: Redraw it with her in silence

column6: Thanks but no worries. The map is still fresh in my mind.
Appreciate it though so don’t beat yourself up.
Well aren’t you a free bird to think 40 minutes lost is nothing of importance?
… Oh. Thank you, I wasn’t expecting that. How nice.
Library, evening. A study carrel by the window; a green lamp; a drawing of a bear in the margin of your notes.
STUDY BREAK — Central Bikol: Yes, No, Have, Have Not. Five items.
Oon means...
Dai means...
Which word means "there is / have"?
Mayo means...
Write "I don't know."
Study Break complete. New: Oon, Dai, Igwa, Mayo, Dai ko aram.
The bear in the margin looks thoughtful. You decide it's a question mark.
Library, night. The reading room is quiet. Nikka is mapping the group's schedule on a blank sheet, murmuring with the pen.
Sain na... sain na ito... Aram ko. Dai ko aram. (frowning) Aram ko... (she crosses out a line) ...Teka.
Ano na naman ito...
(She looks up and notices you.)
Oh. How long were you there?
Dai ko aram. (a small shrug) I think I know the second part. What don't you know?
(very still, then a short exhale) You caught that. (a beat) I just don’t know when I’m free to decide on something. I’ve never been stumped on something before.
Not long. You were talking to the map.
Ah. You saw that. Sorry, I was trying to organize my thoughts there.
Room 401, after rehearsal. You ask Nikka a string of simple questions about the schedule. She decides to answer in the shortest possible way.
Do you have the printouts?
Oon.
Are they in your bag?
Dai.
Then... where?
Oon.
(She isn't smiling. Her eyes are.)
Oon is yes. Dai is no. Correct? (squinting) So I asked "where" and you said "yes." You were messing with me, aren’t you?
(finally laughing) You were supposed to suffer longer.
I need a translator.
(a smile at last) Dai. Finally you finally said something true. Tonight, you better check your Study Notes. It seems to me you’re slacking off of your assignments.
(from her desk) Why is she having fun and I'm not invited?
It seems to me that Nikka finally found her match.
Library, afternoon. Nikka's ledger is open on the table with a calculator, two highlighters, and a receipt for chairs that were never bought.
Jessa. Explain this line item.
It says "motivation money."
It says "motivation money, one thousand pesos."
Inflation!
(not looking up) Jessa, please stop. Nikka has a vein that’s about to burst.
You jest. I am perfectly calm right now.
(She turns to you.)
Secretary. Quick lesson, since you'll be reading receipts for the rest of the semester. Pira? means "how much?" You'll use it at the market. A lot.
Pira.
With a question-like tone. (she lifts her voice at the end) Pira? And if it's an item: Pira ini? How much is this?
(whispering) She gets so alive when it's about money.
I can hear you.
She can hear clearer about money too.
Ask "How much is this?" in Bikol.
Good. In Naga, you would typically say it with a smile and if you’re lucky, they'll lower it by ten pesos. If you’re lucky.
Wrong. It’s Pira ini. You’ll be doomed if you’re in the treasury department.
Would you like a tutor session with Nikka?
Library, evening. The bookshelf. Nikka has laid out a worn street map and three colored pencils.
Now for a professionally run tutoring session. Rule one: I ask questions. Rule two: you may ask me questions back. Rule three: no leading questions. Alright?
Your words for today are as follows: Magayon: beautiful. Igwa: there is or we have. Mayo: none, nothing. They are your Bikolano words for today.
Going back to a previous conversation, another question is “Where” which is Taga-sain.
Let’s apply Where to a sentence. I know where you’re from but what about me?
Ask Nikka where she is from.
Taga-Naga ako. (a smile) You really are a quick learner, aren’t you?
Eh, close. It’s Taga-sain ka? I know you’ll learn it some day.
Room 401, afternoon. Nikka is behind the club table with a ledger, Jessa's receipts, and a face like an auditor's. Inna is annotating a map. Jessa is eating a rice cake that is not hers.

Okay. I can’t believe we’re actually doing a Naga trip just for a project. We don’t have enough funds for such a thing considering the different transportations and the weak tolerance for Jessa's impulsive, so-called club expenses.

Totalling it per person, expenses will be around two thousand nine hundred. It’ll be expensive so nobody should treat it as some kind of vacation. Extra credit will not be awarded to those who only take pictures.
But aren’t pictures THE definitive proof we were actually there?
Well, can you speak in pictures then?
(She turns to you.)
Touche.
You don't have to come. I'm not asking you to be... (a beat, a little defensive) pabigat. But you said you'd pull your weight. So.
How do you answer?

column3: I'll go. I'd like to see where you're from.

column6: (a short blink) You better keep your word. (a half smile) My mom will probably feed you until you beg to stop.
That's an honor.
Mm. (she writes something, then crosses it out) I'll cover the some of the transportation. Don't thank me, it's for the project.
It's kind.
It's for academic purposes.
Sure. But update me ASAP about your decision. I don't like open entries in my ledger.
A riverside market in Naga, morning. Stalls under blue tarps, wet cobbles, a shouting jeepney. Nikka carries a notebook; you carry the recorder.
Before you make a mess of yourself, remember rule one: say tabi before we ask anyone anything. It's how you ask permission and show respect. Say it first.
Tabi po. May we ask a few questions?
(grinning) Aaay, ang polite! Sige, ano yun?
Excuse me po, may we ask a few questions?
Sige, what is it?
Pira ini? (pointing to a bundle of greens)
(delighted) Aaay, talino! (to Nikka) Who is this?
(a little proud, a little embarrassed) The secretary of the club.
Then twenty. For the secretary.
The market is cleaner than it used to be. People still complain now, but I still remember the muddied streets.
(Later, near the jeepney stop.)
Cleaner? It's more crowded! The vendors block the lane. Try driving here during rush hours!.
(Later, on a bench under a tree. A thermos of tea passes between you.)
I miss the old river. We used to wash clothes there but now, it’s nothing more but a memory.
(She hands you a cup.)
Dios mabalos po.
(her whole face lights up) Aaay. You say it properly. Dios mabalos, apo.
(aside) It's old-fashioned. People my age mostly say salamat. But Lola Pilar hears it as sincere.
Thank you po.
(kindly) Hm. Nice manners.
Three people with different opinions. It’s hard to apply daily life when all their lives are lived differently.
How do we handle three accounts?

column3: Include all three, say who said what, with permission.
Pick the most common view and use that.

column6: I agree with your idea. It still shows how people can live different lives and have different ideas, while still expressing with the same language
What we deem as common would add bias into the research, making the results skewed. That’s the wrong approach.
It would have been better if they’re separate summaries. Making an amalgamate of opinion would just dissolve the critical parts of their account.
Write "I don't know yet."
column10: Dai = not; aram = know; pa = yet.

column6: Nikka's family house, early evening. A small table by a window that looks onto the river. Field notes are spread across it. Nikka's mother passes through with a tray and a look that says "eat something."
How do we answer a question with no specific answer? All the evidence we got were varied.

Our question is “How do people live with language in daily life?” We got our answer by seeing how different people express their lives in the same language. We may have gotten a variety of answers, but it still shows how language unites people’s everyday lives.
Then we’ve succeeded with the project?
Not yet. We’ve yet to reflect about what we learned and what we still don't know.
(She looks at the river. Then, lower:)
Magayon.
Beautiful. (a beat) It really is.
(looking at you for a second too long) My grandmother used the word for how a place feels when you stop trying to understand it and just look.
It means beautiful. My grandmother used it for how a place feels when you stop trying to understand it and just look.
Our original question was too simple. It doesn’t discuss the nuances that a language holds for its meaning.
What do you say?

column3: Let's revise it together. We can say what we found and what we still need.
Keep the original claim. It sounds stronger.
If there's no conclusion, what's the point?

column6: (a slow exhale) That’s a wonderful idea.
(She crosses out a line in your draft and writes a new one. She turns the notebook so you can see.)
(very evenly) Sounds stronger but is it relevant? Is it correct?
I thought the presentation needs a clear answer.
Not everything should have a clear answer. That’s what life is.
(quieter) That's what I ask myself about my whole life.
(She says nothing else. The moment hangs, unfinished.)
Naga stalls, night. Stalls closing. A string of bulbs, a rolling shutter, a vendor humming. Nikka sits on an overturned crate with her phone face-down on her knee.
I got an email. Well, three days ago to be specific. I just haven’t opened it still.
What's it about?
It’s a research internship in Manila. I applied on impulse and forgot about it soon after. I wasn’t exxpecting a reply but here I am, faced with confirmation or rejection. I’m not sure what to do.
You apologize with “Pasensya na” and say you were wrong to prefer a stronger-sounding answer.
Thank you. That helps.
What do you do?

column3: Do you want to open it now or later? I'll stay either way.
Just open it! You'll feel better.
Want me to read it first?

column6: (quiet for a while) ...Later. I think I need to know what I'm hoping for before I know what it says.
Want to figure that out together?
You're asking me a question again. (a small smile) Fine. That one I'll allow.
(flat) It doesn't work like that.
(She opens it anyway, reads, closes the phone. Her face gives nothing.)
It's a yes. I don't know if I feel better.
No. It's mine. (firmly, not unkindly) I'll open it when I'm ready.
The last jeepney arrives. The ride back is quiet. Nikka rests her head against the window.
Library, afternoon. Back on campus. A rain-spotted window; the green lamp again.
STUDY BREAK — Central Bikol: Feelings and Thanks. Five items.
Magayon means...
Dios mabalos is used to say...
Maogma ako means...
Write "I don't know yet."
Tabi is used to...
You write a tiny question mark next to each word. It seems like the right punctuation.
Room 401, presentation morning. Nikka has laid out her cue cards in an exact semicircle. Jessa is trying to rearrange them.
Hey. Don't touch those.
I'm decorating.
They aren't a cake.
(calmly, without looking up) Jessa, bay-am.
(immediately sitting) Okay, okay.
(Nikka holds a card, reads it, flips it over, reads the back, and puts it down.)
Nervous?
No. (a beat) I'm... calculating the likelihood of a bad outcome.
We call that nervousness here.
Well. It's a more accurate word to say the least. Don't tell the others though.
What do you say?

column3: Whatever happens, I'll be in the front row.
Just say what you know. That's enough.

column6: (a quick look away) That's not statistically useful.
(But she nods.)
...It might be. Okay.
(looking at the pen) Your pen is jammed.
I know.
(a half smile) I'll use it.
Room 401, presentation day. Nikka's notes are clean. The final slide reads: What We Know, What We Heard, What We Don't Yet Know.
Three people described the same market in three different ways. We don't think one of them is wrong.
After all, life is experienced through different means. Language unites us together, but even then, it won’t help us understand each other.
(She walks through the accounts, with names and permission noted. Then the professor leans forward.)
Your conclusion?
Dai ko pa aram. I don't know yet. Here's what we would need to learn it.
(You catch the Bikol before she translates, and your shoulders loosen. You don't flinch. She sees that.)
(A ripple through the class. The professor's face doesn't change.)
What do you do?

column3: Step in: "We can say what we'd study next."
Jump in with a tidy summary
Stay quiet and let her answer

column6: (grateful, steadying) Next: more interviews, a longer time frame, and people who weren't at the market at all. Context is important in interviews but especially in language.
(nodding slowly) That's an honest answer. Better than a confident wrong one.
What we found is that the market has improved...
(softly) That isn't what we found.
(You see it land. The professor raises a brow.)
(She holds the silence longer than anyone expects. Then she finds the rest of the answer on her own.)
Campus garden, evening. Rain has just stopped; leaves drip. Nikka's campus map is rolled under her arm. She sits on the bench with her back to the wall, as if she has chosen the least likely view.
People keep asking what I'm going to do after graduation, like I owe them a final answer. It’s not that easy to say when there’s a whole world waiting for me.
You can be moving even if you don't know the destination.
And if I change direction?
You choose to turn where your heart takes you. It’s not an aimless change but an exploratory decision.
You’ve turned into somebody clever these past few months. You know the best words to soothe me.
I don't have all the answers either. I’m not as knowledgeable as you.
Good. I'd be suspicious if you did.
After we left, I finally decided to open the email and… I managed to get in. I told my mom through a video call and she managed to cry harder than me. It was so odd.
That sounds like her.
(laughs, a real one) It really does.
Write "I'm happy."
What do you tell her?

column3: I have feelings for you. I'd like to see whether we want to take the next step together.
I value what we've built, even as friends.
Promise you won't change or move away.

column6: Campus garden, evening. A drop of water falls from a leaf onto the notebook.
(a long breath) Oh. For a person who questions a lot of things, I never even thought to think about those sorts of stuff. I thought I was beyond those.
That's fine.
But maybe it was because it felt so natural, that I didn’t realize it was something more.
You mean to say…
Must I spell it out for you, [PLAYER NAME]? Well, long story short, In Other Word, Mahal Kita, [FIRST NAME].
…Maogma ako. Me too. I'm so happy, I mean. (a half-laugh) I said it right, right?
(smiling, then shy) You said it right.
That’s good, because I like you too, Nikka.
Maogma ako. It means "I'm happy." (quieter) I can’t believe we’ve maybe it this far.
Taano? (laughing at herself) Why did it have to be you? Honestly, I can't explain it. Maybe that's the point.
(She unrolls the map. There's a new line on it: from this bench to the edge of the paper.)
Weeks later. A shared photo of the bench in the rain. Caption: "Not finished. Don't fix it."
A MAP WITHOUT ANSWERS (ROMANTIC)
Room 401, a week later. They walk out together, the long way.
I thought about it. I'm not saying no to knowing you. I’m just not sure I see myself in that shoes.
Okay. I'm glad you told me.
It's easier to tell the truth when you're not afraid of how the other person will take it.
A last word

column3: I'll still walk the long way with you.
Can I ask you a question?

column6: Obviously. You'd get lost otherwise.
(arched brow) Taano? (grins) Go on.
THE ROADS WE SHARE (CLASSMATES ONLY)
Campus garden, evening. The same bench. This time Nikka stays standing.
I'm going to be honest, because that's the only way I know. I care about you but I don't feel the same way.
Thank you for telling me honestly.
I’ve always seen us looking at each other eye to eye. But that’s it. Nothing more than equals.
I'd rather give you a clear no than a vague maybe. (a pause) I'm sorry if that hurts.
A last word

column3: It does a little. But I'm glad you said it.
Can we still finish the project?

column6: (a soft breath) Thank you for not pretending it doesn't.
Yes. I'd like that. We make good group after all.
MY OWN DIRECTION (REJECTION)
